---
title: "Configure experiments with Hydra"
---

Hydra and Python are two interfaces to the same package. Hydra composes objects
and manages experiment configuration; `Surrogate` performs training, inference
and persistence. The package does not have separate implementations for these
workflows.

## Packaged configurations

```bash
uv run metis train --cfg job
uv run metis train model=mlp training.steps=1000
uv run metis-train model=flow_matching training.device=cpu training.batch_size=128
```

Run these commands from the uv project created in the
[quickstart](quickstart.qmd). Configurations are included in the wheel, so the
project can live outside the METIS repository. Use `training.device=cuda` after
the quickstart's CUDA setup to select an NVIDIA GPU.
Model groups are `mlp`, `transformer`, `flow_matching` and `itarflow`. The default
dataset is the bundled example. Dimensions are inferred from its schema.

For your data:

```bash
uv run metis train dataset=parquet dataset.path=/absolute/path/bank.parquet 'dataset.inputs=[contact_rate,recovery_rate]' 'dataset.outputs=[incidence,prevalence]'
```

A dataset factory can also return a `DatasetSplit` for explicitly prepared
partitions. Hydra's `_target_` composition lets experienced users supply their
own importable factory without replacing METIS's training loop. Relative
Parquet paths are resolved from the launch directory, even with
`hydra.job.chdir=true`.

## Sweeps

```bash
uv run metis train --multirun model=mlp,transformer training.learning_rate=0.001,0.0003 evaluation.partition=validation
```

Each run writes its resolved configuration, complete model, training history and
evaluation metrics into its own directory. Changing a model changes its training
objective; compare shared original-unit validation metrics instead of ranking
unrelated training losses. After choosing the model/settings, assess the
independent test bank once. Using test metrics to select a sweep winner would
make those results tuning performance rather than a final test.

Set `plot.enabled=true` with the `[plots]` extra for a diagnostic figure. Add it
to your project with
`uv add "metis-surrogate[plots] @ git+https://github.com/OJWatson/metis.git"`,
including any other extras you already use in the same requirement. A
multirun job that still uses `evaluation.partition=test` emits a warning: it does
not automatically change the partition or conceal evaluation choices.

## Live Weights & Biases tracking

Tracking is optional and off by default. Install the `[wandb]` extra to stream
training loss at every optimizer step, validation loss when evaluated, and final
evaluation metrics. Hydra and Python use the same progress callback.

```bash
uv add "metis-surrogate[wandb] @ git+https://github.com/OJWatson/metis.git"
# Local tracking; no account, credentials, or network required:
uv run metis train training.steps=100 wandb.enabled=true wandb.mode=offline
```

If you also use plots or pandas tables, include those extras in the requirement,
for example `[plots,pandas,wandb]`. uv records the selection, so tracking remains
available on subsequent `uv run` calls.

For an online run, authenticate with `uv run wandb login`, then select the project and,
if appropriate, your user or team entity:

```bash
uv run metis train wandb.enabled=true wandb.project=my-surrogate-study wandb.entity=my-team
```

Do not put credentials in YAML or commit them to the repository. W&B manages
authentication; METIS passes project settings to the installed W&B client.

Tracking logs the supplied configuration and scalar training/evaluation metrics.
It does **not** automatically upload simulation tables, predictions, or model
files. Configurations may contain local data paths and column names. Local METIS
model and evaluation artifacts are saved independently of tracking.

The same adapter works in a notebook or script:

```python
from dataclasses import asdict
from metis import load_example, Surrogate, TrainingConfig
from metis.tracking import WandbTracker

split = load_example().split(seed=42)
config = TrainingConfig(steps=100, eval_every=20)
with WandbTracker(
    project="my-surrogate-study",
    mode="offline",  # Change to online after configuring W&B authentication.
    config={"model": "mlp", "training": asdict(config)},
    dir="tracking",
) as tracking:
    surrogate = Surrogate("mlp").fit(
        split.train, split.validation, config=config,
        on_progress=tracking.log_training,
    )
    report = surrogate.evaluate(split.test)
    tracking.log_evaluation(report, prefix="test")
    surrogate.save("surrogate.pt")
    report.save("evaluation.json")
```

The context closes runs on success or failure. `WandbTracker(enabled=False)` is
a no-op and does not import or require W&B. A custom `on_progress` callback can
instead update a dashboard or another logger; it receives a copied dictionary
with `step`, `train_loss` and, on validation steps, `validation_loss`.

## Existing source recipes

The original `train.py` and configs remain available for advanced CUDA/DDP and
sequence-conditioning experiments with `[legacy]` installed. New experiments
using static inputs should use `uv run metis train` so Python and Hydra share portable
artifacts and scientific diagnostics. Historical checkpoints cannot be loaded
by `Surrogate.load`; their normalization was not bundled. Preserve the original
bank when using those old checkpoints.
